title: Karlsson-on-the-Roof
author: Astrid Lindgren
short_summary: Svante Svantesson, a seven-year-old everybody calls Kid, lives in an ordinary flat in an ordinary Stockholm street with his parents, his big brother Bosse and his big sister Bettan. Then a small, plump, extremely pleased-with-himself man flies in at his window. Karlsson lives in a little house on the roof, starts the propeller on his back with a button on his stomach, is the world's best at absolutely everything, and never once takes the blame.
extended_summary:
Kid is the youngest in the family and would rather have a friend, or a dog, than almost anything. What arrives instead is Karlsson-on-the-Roof: a very short, very round little man who lives in a house hidden behind a chimney, presses a button on his stomach to start the propeller on his back, and treats Kid's bedroom as a place to visit whenever he feels like it.

Karlsson announces before nearly every attempt that he is the world's best at whatever it is — the world's best steam-engine engineer, the world's best cake-eater, the world's best rooster-crower. Then the steam engine explodes, or the buns disappear, or the shelf comes off the wall, and Karlsson says that it is a trifle, an everyday matter, and flies off before anybody can ask questions. Kid is left to explain to his mother.

No grown-up ever quite believes in him. Kid's parents think he has invented Karlsson, which makes the friendship a strange, private thing: the one person who is completely on Kid's side is also the one who gets him into all the trouble. And when Kid's birthday finally comes and the dog he has wanted for years is really there, Karlsson arrives too, because he is not going to miss a party — and because Kid, unlike anybody else in the book, has always been glad to see him.

questions.prompt: How does Karlsson get himself off the ground?

options: A button on his stomach starts a propeller on his back
He takes a run at the window and jumps a long way
He holds an umbrella above his head and the wind lifts him
He whistles and a machine pulls him up from the roof

questions.explanation: Propeller on the back, starter button on the stomach — and no explanation of where he got it. Lindgren puts one impossible machine into an ordinary Stockholm flat, and then behaves as though nothing needed explaining at all.

options: In a little house on the roof, behind a chimney
In an attic room at the top of Kid's building
In a cupboard in the corner of Kid's bedroom
In a workshop under the stairs of the house

questions.explanation: Behind a chimney, where nobody would ever think to look and where no grown-up ever climbs. It is exactly the sort of place a seven-year-old would choose to believe in — near enough to reach, high enough that nobody can check.

questions.prompt: Karlsson describes himself, more than once, as a handsome, thoroughly clever and perfectly plump man in the ___ of life.
questions.explanation: He says it whenever anyone doubts him, and occasionally when nobody has said anything at all. The joke lasts the entire series because it is exactly how a small child imagines a grown-up sounds when boasting.

questions.prompt: Something of Kid's has just been broken, spilled or eaten. What does Karlsson say?

options: That it is a trifle — an everyday sort of matter
That Kid should have put it somewhere safer
That he will pay for it out of his own money
That the two of them should keep it a secret

questions.explanation: It is his answer to every disaster, and he is always the one who caused it. The phrase is so useful that children who read the book start saying it themselves — which is, presumably, exactly what Lindgren intended.

questions.prompt: Karlsson's visits nearly always go the same way. Put the stages in order.

items: A buzzing noise comes in through Kid's window
Karlsson announces he is the world's best at it
The thing goes spectacularly wrong at once
Karlsson explains that it is a trifle
He presses his button and flies away over the roofs
Kid is left to explain the mess to his mother

questions.explanation: The pattern repeats so exactly that a reader can predict it by the third chapter — and that is the pleasure of it. Notice the order of the last two: Karlsson always leaves before the consequences arrive.

questions.prompt: Match each member of Kid's world to who they are.

right: The dog Kid has wanted for years
The neighbour nobody grown-up believes in

questions.explanation: Kid has a perfectly nice family and is still lonely in it: two much older siblings with their own lives, two busy parents, and no one his own size. Karlsson and Bimbo fill the same gap from opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Sort each statement by who it is true of.

options.label: Is seven years old and the youngest at home
Has been asking for a dog for a very long time
Gets told off for the mess after every visit
Lives alone in a house nobody can find
Is the world's best at whatever comes up
Has never once apologised for anything

questions.explanation: Everything in the right-hand column is something a seven-year-old might wish for: your own house, no adults, complete confidence, and no consequences. Karlsson is not just Kid's friend — he is a fairly exact picture of what Kid would like to be.

questions.prompt: Karlsson eats Kid's sweets, breaks his things and leaves him to be told off. Why does Kid keep wanting him to come back?

options: Karlsson is the only one who is never too busy for him
Karlsson has promised to take him flying one day
Kid is frightened of what Karlsson would do otherwise
Karlsson has been paying him back a little at a time

questions.explanation: Kid's parents are kind and occupied, his brother and sister are teenagers, and Karlsson turns up wanting to play. Lindgren never says this out loud — she simply shows a small boy alone in a room, and then shows him laughing.

questions.prompt: Karlsson eats more than his share, breaks things, boasts constantly and lets Kid take the blame. Is he a good friend to Kid, or a bad one? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both verdicts can earn full marks. A strong 'bad friend' answer lists what Karlsson actually does and notices that he always leaves before the trouble lands. A strong 'good friend' answer notices that he comes when Kid is alone, that he treats Kid as an equal, and that Kid is happier with him than without. The best answers manage to say both at once.

questions.prompt: Karlsson declares that he is the world's best at something before he tries it — and then makes a complete mess of it. Invent one more: what would he announce he is the world's best at, what would he actually do, and how would it go wrong?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong invention keeps all three of Lindgren's beats: the boast first, the attempt second, the disaster third — and ideally Karlsson escaping before anyone can blame him. A boast with no disaster after it is only half the joke.

questions.prompt: There is one thing Kid wants for his birthday more than anything else in the world: a ___.
questions.explanation: He asks for it for years and is told there is no room. When Bimbo finally arrives, the moment is given as much weight as any of Karlsson's flying — Lindgren knows exactly how large a small wish can be.

questions.prompt: What do the grown-ups in Kid's family think about Karlsson?

options: They believe Kid has invented him
They have asked him not to come back again
They think he is a boy from the flat upstairs
They have complained to the police about him

questions.explanation: For most of the book the adults treat Karlsson as an imaginary friend, which leaves Kid in the odd position of being blamed for real damage caused by someone nobody admits exists. It is also why the friendship feels private — it belongs to Kid alone.
